prerequisites: Successful completion of the courses Psychology of Education, Pedagogy I, and Pedagogy II.
Learning outcomes specific to the courses Psychology of Education, Pedagogy I, and Pedagogy II.

learning_outcomes.text: Knows, understands, and uses specialized language.
Correlates specialized and psycho-pedagogical knowledge in carrying out instructive-educational activities in education and other educational activities.
Argues the formative potential of theories, principles, and specific didactic practices in the field.
Observes and evaluates students' school and social behaviors.
Constructs authentic learning contexts, in an integrated manner, where students valorize their life experiences and cognitive interests.
Responsibly executes professional tasks under conditions of limited autonomy and qualified assistance.
Develops creative and constructive attitudes in applying didactic principles.
Indicates the necessity of using varied resources for teaching efficiency, supporting learning, and helping students use them autonomously.
Communicates effectively by providing constructive feedback and supports students' active involvement in their own learning process.

syllabus_topics: I. Didactics and the teaching-learning process
I.I Characteristics of the teaching-learning process.
1.2. Didactics - general theory of the teaching-learning process.
1.3. Subject of study of didactics.
I.4. The connection of didactics with teaching methodologies for disciplines.
1.5. Place and role of domain disciplines in pre-university education.
II. Application of the new curriculum for domain disciplines
2.1. Definitions and conceptions of curriculum.
2.2. National Curriculum.
2.3. Curricular cycles of education.
2.4. School documents (Framework curriculum plans, School programs, School manual).
III. Educational objectives in the instruction process
3.1. Levels of defining educational objectives.
3.2. Functions of educational objectives.
3.3. Framework objectives, reference objectives, operational objectives.
3.4. General competencies, specific competencies, and contents.
3.5. Transposing competencies into operational objectives.
3.6. Methodology for operationalizing objectives. Operationalization techniques.
IV. Teaching methods specific to domain disciplines
4.1. Definition of concepts: didactic technology, didactic strategy, didactic methodology, teaching methods, didactic procedures.
4.2. Classification of teaching methods used in teaching domain disciplines.
4.2.1. Oral communication learning methods. Expository methods.
4.2.2. Oral communication learning methods. Interrogative methods.
4.2.3. Written communication learning methods.
4.2.4. Reality exploration learning methods.
4.2.5. Action-based learning methods.
4.2.5.1. Real action-based learning methods.
4.2.5.2. Fictional action-based learning methods.
4.2.6. Methods for rationalizing learning and teaching.
V. Teaching aids specific to domain disciplines
5.1. Definition of teaching aids.
5.2. Didactic functions of teaching aids.
5.3. Types of teaching aids and their characteristics.
5.4. Description of the learning environment.
5.5. Equipping the learning environment.
VI. Forms of organization and conduct of instruction activities
6.1 Organization of the didactic process by classes and lessons for domain disciplines.
6.2. Types of lessons specific to domain disciplines.
6.3. Other forms of organization of the didactic process that can be addressed within domain disciplines.
6.3.1. Didactic excursions and visits.
6.3.2. Practical work in workshops and laboratories.
6.3.3. Student clubs.
6.3.4. Didactic consultations.
6.3.5. Didactic tutoring.
VII. Evaluation in the teaching-learning process
7.1. Concept of evaluating the teaching-learning process.
7.2. Objectives. Functions.
7.3. Types of evaluations. Characterization.
7.4. Traditional evaluation methods.
7.5. Modern evaluation methods.
7.6. Qualities of evaluation instruments.
7.7. Item typology.
VIII. Designing the didactic approach for the technology curricular area
8.1 Personalized reading of school curricula.
8.2. Indicative calendar planning.
8.3. Designing the learning unit.
8.4. Designing the lesson.
IX. Teacher preparation for classroom activity
9.1 Functions exercised by the teacher in classroom activity.
9.2. Methodological competencies of the teaching staff.
Seminar Activity
1. The role and importance of technical disciplines in the teaching-learning process.
2. The finalities of studying domain disciplines.
3. Analysis of framework plans and school curricula specific to domain disciplines.
4. Analysis of school textbooks.
5. Planning of didactic activity. Annual calendar planning (Semester planning).
6. Planning of didactic activity. Designing the learning unit.
7. Planning of didactic activity. Designing lesson plans (by types).
8. Deepening the succession of lesson events. Developing the structure of a specialized lesson for various types or variants of lessons.
9. Development of evaluation sequences and tests.
10. The role of the technical department, the specialized cabinet, and tutoring activity in the system of instruction activities.
11. Simulation of trial lessons.

assessment_methods.method: Systematic observation of students (individual/team assignments, preparation of a report/case study)
Formative evaluation test (checks during the semester)

assessment_rules: The student passes the course if they demonstrate understanding of the principles and methods of planning, organizing, and evaluating the instructive-educational process and can apply them correctly in didactic contexts. A minimum final grade of 5 is required. Additionally, a minimum score of 5 is required for the 'Examen' component and the 'Aplicatii' component.
